Happy to. Here's the core set:

**Reorder point (ROP)** = (average daily demand × lead time) + safety stock

**Safety stock** = z × σ_d × √L (σ_d = std dev of daily demand, L = lead time in days, z = service-level factor)

**Common z values:** 90% → 1.28, 95% → 1.65, 99% → 2.33

**EOQ** = √(2DS / H) (D = annual demand, S = order cost, H = annual holding cost per unit)

Quick example: demand 50/day, σ_d = 10, lead time 4 days, 95% service. Safety stock = 1.65 × 10 × 2 = 33. ROP = 50 × 4 + 33 = 233 units.

table pls. im a logistics management junior so i should know this but dr ashby covered a ton of stuff tuesday in th final review and my notes are a mess

| Concept | Formula | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| Reorder point | d × L + SS | Deciding when to place an order |
| Safety stock | z × σ_d × √L | Demand varies, lead time fixed |
| Safety stock (variable lead time) | z × √(L·σ_d² + d²·σ_L²) | Both demand and lead time vary |
| EOQ | √(2DS/H) | Balancing order vs. holding cost |
| Cycle service level | P(demand during lead time ≤ ROP) | Picking z |
| Inventory turnover | COGS / avg inventory | Comparing efficiency |

Tip: if a problem gives weekly demand but daily lead time, convert units first. That's the classic exam trap.

How students typically prep for quantitative finals like this:
- Redo practice problems from scratch rather than rereading solutions
- Make a one-page formula sheet, then test whether you can rebuild it from memory
- Do a timed mixed set so you practice picking the right formula
- Explain each concept aloud in a sentence or two
